questions.stem: Which newspaper, founded in 1780 by James Augustus Hicky, was the first newspaper published in India?

options.option_text: The Hindu (Chennai)
Hicky's Bengal Gazette
Amrita Bazar Patrika
Bombay Samachar (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: Hicky's Bengal Gazette (also called Calcutta General Advertiser) was the first newspaper printed in India, published from January 1780 by James Augustus Hicky. It was independent and often critical of the East India Company, leading to Hicky's imprisonment.

questions.stem: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, passed during Lord Lytton's tenure, was enacted to suppress Indian-language newspapers. Which Viceroy repealed this act in 1882?

options.option_text: Lord Curzon
Lord Dufferin
Lord Ripon
Lord Elgin

questions.explanation: The Vernacular Press Act (1878), nicknamed the 'Gagging Act', gave magistrates broad powers to suppress Indian-language newspapers. Lord Ripon, known for liberal reforms, repealed it in 1882 as part of his policy to ease colonial repression and gain Indian support.

questions.stem: The Amrita Bazar Patrika, founded in 1868, adopted a clever strategy to escape the Vernacular Press Act of 1878. What did it do?

options.option_text: It moved its printing press from Calcutta to Bombay beyond Bengal jurisdiction
It published coded messages in Sanskrit that the colonial censors could not understand
It merged with an English paper already exempt under pre-existing colonial press laws
It switched overnight from Bengali to English publication to remain outside the Act's scope

questions.explanation: When the Vernacular Press Act (1878) was imminent, the Amrita Bazar Patrika (founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh) converted overnight from a bilingual Bengali-English paper to a fully English publication. Since the Act applied only to vernacular (Indian-language) newspapers, the Patrika successfully evaded its provisions.

questions.stem: Bal Gangadhar Tilak used two newspapers — Kesari (in Marathi) and Mahratta (in English) — to spread nationalist ideas. Tilak was convicted of sedition in 1897 for articles that the British claimed incited violence. Which article led to this conviction?

options.option_text: Articles on Shivaji's killing of Afzal Khan as an act of justified patriotism
Reports on the Jallianwala Bagh massacre demanding immediate independence
Editorials criticising the partition of Bengal as a colonial conspiracy
Columns advocating the armed overthrow of the Morley-Minto reforms

questions.explanation: In 1897, Tilak wrote articles in Kesari glorifying Shivaji's killing of Afzal Khan as a historical parallel for resisting oppression. The British used these as grounds for a sedition charge under Section 124A IPC. Tilak was convicted and sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment. He called himself 'the father of Indian unrest.'

questions.stem: Which Indian social reformer and newspaper editor founded the 'Dina Mani' and 'Swadesamitran' newspapers in Tamil to spread reform ideas in southern India?

options.option_text: Subramania Bharati (poet and freedom fighter)
Periyar E. V. Ramasamy (social reform leader)
G. Subramania Iyer (Tamil nationalist journalist)
C. Rajagopalachari (the statesman and writer)

questions.explanation: G. Subramania Iyer founded Swadesamitran (1882, Tamil) and The Hindu (1878, English) to promote nationalist and reform ideas in South India. Swadesamitran became one of the most influential Tamil-language newspapers of the freedom movement era.

questions.stem: The Newspaper (Incitement to Offences) Act of 1908, passed after the Muzaffarpur bombing, gave colonial authorities power to seize printing presses. Against which publication was this act first invoked?

options.option_text: Bipin Chandra Pal's New India magazine in Calcutta
Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Kesari newspaper in Pune
Aurobindo Ghosh's Yugantar revolutionary journal
Annie Besant's New India journal in Madras

questions.explanation: After the Muzaffarpur bomb case (1908), the colonial government passed the Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act and used it to seize Tilak's printing presses in Pune. Tilak was prosecuted for sedition again (his second trial) and sentenced to 6 years' transportation to Mandalay, Burma.

questions.stem: The Indian Press Act of 1910 required newspaper publishers to deposit a security that could be forfeited if the publication was deemed seditious. Which Viceroy introduced this act and why is this period considered a high point of colonial press censorship?

options.option_text: Lord Hardinge II, reacting to Gandhiji's first non-cooperation movement campaign
Lord Chelmsford, implementing the Rowlatt Act committee's press censorship recommendations
Lord Reading, responding to the Khilafat movement's anti-government newspaper campaign
Lord Minto II, responding to the revolutionary surge following the partition of Bengal (1905)

questions.explanation: The Indian Press Act (1910) was introduced under Lord Minto II (Viceroy 1905–1910) as part of a crackdown on revolutionary nationalism that surged after the partition of Bengal (1905). Publishers had to deposit large securities (up to Rs 2,000); forfeiture effectively silenced smaller nationalist papers. It gave the colonial government broad discretion to punish 'seditious' publications without judicial oversight.
